title: NSSI as Inward-Routed Mobilization: Over-Idealized Figures and State Transition
content: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is often described through functional labels such as emotion regulation, self-punishment, interpersonal influence, or escape from aversive internal states. These labels are clinically useful, but they do not fully explain how self-injury becomes selected under stress. This paper proposes the Inward-Routed Mobilization Model (IRM) of NSSI, a mechanism-level account of selection under high activation, reduced deployable capacity, and constrained outward representation. IRM suggests that NSSI becomes more likely when mobilization rises, negative affect cannot be safely represented toward an over-idealized figure, outward expression is appraised as relationally or psychologically dangerous, and the body becomes the most immediate site for state change. The pathway does not require consciously labeled anger; it requires that protest, hurt, disappointment, shame, humiliation, or boundary-relevant mobilization cannot be safely directed toward the protected figure. The model is organized around a common origin pathway: over-idealized figure constraint, truncated negative affective mobilization, inward routing, and bodily state transition. IRM adds a selection-level account to existing functional, reinforcement, self-punishment, and emotion-regulation models and yields testable predictions for ecological momentary assessment, developmental research, clinical formulation, and treatment studies focused on constraint repair, capacity restoration, and safe outward throughput.
